name: PA66 (Nylon 6,6)
chemical_makeup: Aliphatic polyamide condensation copolymer of hexamethylenediamine and adipic acid — two alternating six-carbon units rather than PA6's single ring-opened caprolactam repeat. The symmetric repeat packs into a tighter, higher-melting crystal (~255-265 °C vs PA6's ~220 °C), which is the origin of its extra stiffness, wear resistance and heat resistance, and of its extra shrinkage.
summary: The stiff, hot, hard-to-tame nylon. Deltas vs the base pa entry and vs pa6: melting point and processing temperatures climb (255-275 °C for low-warp grades, 285-315 °C and a 130 °C bed for high-performance grades), density rises to ~1.14, stiffness, wear resistance and creep resistance all improve, and service temperature reaches ~135 °C — while hygroscopicity stays as bad as PA6's and shrinkage gets worse. Rarer than PA6 on the hobby market and more expensive; many spools labelled 'PA6/66' are deliberately easier-printing copolymer blends rather than this homopolymer.

printing.notes: The widest nozzle window in this family and the largest unresolved disagreement: ABC3D's low-warp PA66 runs 255-275 °C on a 60-70 °C bed, while its high-performance PA66 wants 285-315 °C on a 130 °C bed — a spread that almost certainly reflects different formulations (possibly filled) rather than one material, so check the specific datasheet before trusting the recommended 275 °C. Deltas vs pa6: hotter at both ends, a hotter bed for the high-performance grades, and a slightly wider fan allowance (ABC3D permits 0-30 %, unusual for a nylon) — but 0 % remains the safe starting point since fan air amplifies this grade's already-high shrinkage. Enclosure effectively mandatory; ambient targeted a little higher than pa6 because of the higher melt point. Unfilled PA66 is not abrasive, so no hardened nozzle — a PA66-CF product does exist (ABC3D) and would require one.

feeding.notes: Rigid, unfilled and mechanically easy to push, so any extruder feeds it; no shore hardness and no feeding assistant (not an elastomer). Standard hobbed drive gears are sufficient — there is no filler to wear them, unlike the CF/GF grades. AMS status is 'conditional' on the same moisture grounds as pa6: ABC3D describes PA66 as absorbing ambient moisture 'in just a few hours', so only a sealed, actively desiccated unit is acceptable and a heated drybox is better. No Bambu-branded pure PA66 exists, so there is no vendor AMS listing to cite for this grade (unverified).

methods: print directly from a heated dryer
sealed drybox with desiccant while printing
drying.dryness_validation: No popping, crackling or steam at the nozzle; a glossy, blister-free purge line; stringing back to baseline. Because PA66 re-absorbs within hours of opening, validate immediately before the print rather than after drying — a spool that passed yesterday will not necessarily pass today.
drying.notes: Hotter but shorter than pa6's schedule: ABC3D specifies 90 °C for 4 h for both its low-warp and high-performance PA66 lines (alternatively 85 °C for 4-6 h). This is the second-highest drying temperature in the family, behind ppa's 100-140 °C and well above pa12's 70 °C / 4 h — the single clearest ranking of the four grades. Do not assume PA66's higher melting point implies better moisture stability: it does not, and this is the most common misconception about the grade.

storage.recommendations: Airtight with fresh desiccant, opened only at the moment of use. ABC3D warns that PA66 picks up ambient moisture in a few hours, so treat a heated drybox on the printer as the operating state and re-dry any spool that has spent a session in open air.

price.notes: Split by grade: ABC3D's low-warp PA66 is CAD $59.95/kg (~$44 USD/kg) while its high-performance PA66 is $99.95/kg (~$73 USD/kg) — the latter above Bambu's filled PA6-GF pricing, reflecting a rarer resin supply chain and less competition. PA6/66 copolymer blends undercut both at ~$46/kg (Inslogic). USD conversions are approximate and unverified against current rates.

recommended: precision gears, bearings and wear surfaces (low creep under load)
automotive under-hood and high-heat mechanical parts
jigs, fixtures and tooling needing stiffness at temperature
not_recommended: printing without an enclosure — warps at least as badly as pa6
humid or outdoor service without sealing
budget projects (costs more than pa6 for a harder print)
beginners' first nylon — pa12 or a PA6/66 blend is the gentler entry point
parts needing maximum impact toughness or elongation (pa12 is more ductile)
hotends limited to 250-260 °C, which cannot reach the high-performance grades

properties.notes: Density is recorded at the literature homopolymer value of 1.14 g/cm³ — the heaviest unfilled grade in this family, consistent with PA66's tighter crystal packing — but the two product datasheets found read higher still (ABC3D low-warp 1.24, high-performance 1.19), which strongly suggests mineral or glass content in those formulations; see conflicts. Max service temp 135 °C with a service floor of -45 °C (ABC3D high-performance), the widest usable band of the four grades. Tg ~70 °C and HDT@0.45 MPa ~90 °C are literature figures for dry unfilled PA66, both modestly above pa6's 60 °C / 85 °C; as with all nylons they fall as the part takes up water. Tensile 55-85 MPa spans the grades; an Inslogic PA6/66 copolymer blend measures 79 MPa tensile and 103 MPa flexural but with a melt point of only 198 °C, confirming it is not this homopolymer. Shrinkage is reasoned upward from the base pa entry on crystallinity grounds, not a datasheet value.

compatibility.notes: Welds to itself and to the aliphatic polyamide family; the PA66/PA6 pair is the strongest cross-grade bond here because their nozzle windows overlap most, while PA66/PA12 is the weakest of the family pairings given the ~80 °C melt-point gap. No bond to pla, petg, abs, asa, pc, pp, pctg, pvb or pet. Soluble supports are out — pva and bvoh both degrade well below 275 °C — so same-material breakaway supports are standard. Build-plate chemistry is the practical adhesion story: a PA-specific adhesive or glue stick as a promoter, and a garolite sheet for anything large.

plate_recommendations.notes: Usable with a PA adhesive, but the weakest recommendation of the four grades: PA66's higher shrinkage plus bed temperatures up to 130 °C on the high-performance line make edge lift likelier than with pa6, and standard textured PEI sheets are not comfortable at the top of that bed range. Garolite / G10 is the safer surface for pure PA66 and for any large footprint; the low-warp and PA6/66-blend products are more forgiving and may hold on textured PEI with adhesive alone (unverified — two ABC3D datasheets were still marked 'coming soon'). No garolite plate entry exists in the catalog yet, so it is recorded here in notes.
Backfilled from plate entry (Phase E reciprocity): High shrinkage plus unreliable PEI bond; use garolite.
Backfilled from plate entry (Phase E reciprocity): High shrinkage; garolite preferred.

emissions.notes: Same amide-family VOC and ultrafine-particle profile as pa6, but likely worse in practice because the high-performance grades run at 285-315 °C — well above pa6's 220-270 °C — and nylon emissions scale steeply with nozzle temperature. Note the one chemistry delta: PA66 is not a caprolactam source (that is PA6's monomer), so a spool that smells strongly of caprolactam is probably a PA6/66 blend. Source-capture extraction is recommended and becomes near-essential at the top of the temperature range. No PA66-specific emissions measurement was found; this is general nylon-family guidance scaled for temperature (unverified).

safety_notes: The high-performance grades need an all-metal hotend rated well past 300 °C — pushing a PTFE-lined hotend to 315 °C degrades the liner and releases fluoropolymer decomposition products. Keep drying at or below 90 °C to avoid deforming spools. Annealed PA66 parts harden noticeably and become ductile again as they re-absorb humidity; account for that before machining or tapping. Not food-contact suitable.
additional_notes: Read the label carefully with this grade: a large share of filament sold as 'PA66' or 'PA6/66' is a copolymer blend engineered to reduce warping and improve layer adhesion, and it prints far more easily than homopolymer PA66 — the giveaway is a melt point near 198 °C and a bed temperature around 50 °C rather than 100-130 °C. This entry describes the homopolymer. Against its siblings PA66 is the stiffness-and-heat choice among the aliphatic grades: better wear resistance and creep resistance than pa6, far more heat capability than pa12, and none of ppa's hardware requirements — at the cost of being the hardest of the three to keep flat and dry.

provenance.conflicts: Confidence is 'low' because pure single-resin PA66 filament is rare and the available sources conflict badly. Nozzle temperature spans 255-275 °C (ABC3D low-warp) against 285-315 °C (ABC3D high-performance) with bed 60-70 °C against 130 °C — it is unverified which represents 'pure' PA66 and whether the high-performance grade is filled. Density likewise: literature unfilled PA66 is 1.14 g/cm³ but both ABC3D products read 1.19-1.24, implying additives; 1.14 is recorded as the homopolymer value and the product figures are flagged rather than averaged in. Tg (70 °C), HDT (90 °C) and shrinkage are literature/reasoned values, not figures from a filament datasheet. Products sold as 'PA6/66' are copolymer blends with a 198 °C melt point and materially easier printing — their numbers are cited here for contrast only, not merged into this entry. No filled PA66-CF/GF datasheet was obtained (ABC3D lists such a product); flag for follow-up. Emissions and AMS behaviour for PA66 specifically are inferred from PA6, not measured.
